title: How to dictate new paragraph and punctuation on Mac: step by step for macOS 27
metaTitle: Dictate new paragraph and punctuation on Mac: step by step
description: Say “new paragraph” or “new line” and punctuation names to dictate on a Mac. Fix auto-punctuation that misfires, using Apple’s own commands and settings.
targetKeyword: how to dictate new paragraph and punctuation on Mac
intro: To dictate a new paragraph on Mac, say “new paragraph”. Apple treats it as pressing Return twice, and the break appears when you finish dictating. For punctuation, say the mark name, like “comma” or “question mark”. If auto-punctuation guesses wrong, turn it off in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation.
tldr: Say “new line” for one Return and “new paragraph” for two.
Say punctuation by name, such as “comma”, “period”, or “question mark”.
Auto-punctuation adds commas and periods on its own. Turn it off in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation if it misfires.
Dictate in Word needs Microsoft 365. Nuance stopped supporting Dragon for Mac in 2018.
Read every dictated draft once for marks and breaks before you send it.

blocks.text: How to dictate a new paragraph on Mac

Say “new line” for a single break and “new paragraph” for a blank line between blocks of text. Apple’s Commands for dictating text page lists both under Formatting, not Punctuation. A new line works like pressing Return once. A new paragraph works like pressing Return twice. The break appears when you finish dictating.

rows: period, point, dot, or full stop
blocks.caption: Breaks and marks from Apple’s Commands for dictating text page.

blocks.text: Speak the command at the spot where the break belongs. Finish the sentence before it first. Then say the command and keep going. A command said in the middle of a sentence splits that sentence where you did not plan.
Dictating punctuation by name

Apple’s Commands page lists the punctuation names Dictation understands. The list includes comma, period, question mark, exclamation mark, colon, semicolon, ellipsis, dash, hyphen, quote, end quote, and open or close parenthesis, bracket, and brace. Each name produces the matching symbol.

items: period, point, dot, or full stop each give a period
question mark gives a question mark
colon and semicolon give those marks
quote and end quote open and close a quotation
dash and hyphen are separate commands, so say the one you need

blocks.text: Say mark names one at a time. Speak “Thanks for the notes comma I will send the draft Friday period” and each mark lands where you said it. A word you meant as text can also match a command, so check those spots after you dictate.
A worked example: a short note with a paragraph break

Say this in one pass: “Thanks for the notes comma I will send the draft Friday period new paragraph Next comma can we book the review question mark.” The text should read as two paragraphs. The first says “Thanks for the notes, I will send the draft Friday.” The second says “Next, can we book the review?” If the break is missing, you spoke the wrong command or the engine misread it.

blocks.title: Test in a blank note first
blocks.text: Dictate the example above into a blank note. Check each mark and the blank line between the two paragraphs. Only then move to a real document.
Auto-punctuation: what it does and how to turn it off

Auto-punctuation inserts commas, periods, and question marks as you dictate. Apple says this runs in supported languages. You can turn it off in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Apple’s page does not list which languages are supported, so check that before you rely on the feature.

Auto-punctuation misfires most when your speech is long and uneven. Research on long-form dictation says irregular pauses and slow speakers cause segmentation and punctuation problems. Third-party guides also say auto-punctuation is unreliable on long sentences. I could not confirm that on Apple’s page.

blocks.title: Check your Mac before you trust the setting
blocks.text: Apple documents an on-device model that improves spelling, punctuation, and capitalization in English. It needs an M3 or later Mac with at least 12GB of unified memory, on macOS 27. Older Macs may behave differently, and Apple’s page does not say how.
Fixing line breaks that land in the wrong place

Fix a break with the keyboard. Put the cursor after the break and press Delete (⌫) to remove one Return. Press Return to add one back. Re-check the spacing after each change, since one edit can shift the lines below it.
Word, Dictate, and the Auto Punctuation setting

Microsoft’s Dictate in Word page says the feature is only available to Microsoft 365 subscribers. It covers Word for Microsoft 365 on Windows and Mac. Start it from Home > Dictate. The Auto Punctuation setting sits under the gear icon in the dictation settings.

Auto Punctuation changes only if it is available for the language you picked. Microsoft also says preview languages may have lower accuracy or limited punctuation support. Check the language list before you dictate a long document. Our [Word for writers guide](/for/writers/word) covers document setup.
Pages and Google Docs: what I could and could not verify

I checked Apple’s Dictation and Commands pages for the Mac side. I did not find a source for Pages-specific or Google Docs-specific dictation commands, so this guide does not describe them. Test the commands in a blank document first and read the result. The Pages guide is at [Pages for writers on Mac](/for/writers/pages).
What the research says about speed and errors

In a lab study of short messages on an iPhone 6 Plus, English speech averaged 153 words per minute. The keyboard averaged 52. Speech left more errors in the final text, 1.30% against 0.79%. The task was short messages, not proofread documents, so read the numbers as a direction, not a forecast.

A randomized trial of physicians found speech-assisted reports were longer, 649 characters per report against 356. The authors suggest the bigger effect may be more documentation, not time saved. More text means more marks and breaks to check. Read the whole draft once more before you send it.
Edge cases and common mistakes

items: Saying “period” in a sentence about a span of time, when you meant a full stop
Using “dash” when you need a hyphen in a word like well-known
Leaving auto-punctuation on for lists, addresses, or code, where marks change the meaning
Dictating a list as one sentence, so every item runs into the next
Using “new paragraph” for every break, which adds gaps you do not want
Skipping the read-through because the draft sounded right when you spoke it

blocks.text: If your work involves client or patient records, follow your employer’s rules on which tools you may use and what data they may process. Do not dictate records into a tool your employer has not approved.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur’s hold fn dictation types clean, formatted text at your cursor in any app. You can save snippets for text you repeat, and keep a personal dictionary for names. Lazur does not click buttons or change settings for you. It explains, points, and guides you one click at a time.

The fastest use for this problem is a question. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Auto-punctuation is, or how to start a new paragraph in the app you have open. Lazur answers out loud. Test any formatting it gives you in a blank note before a real draft.
A short routine to make the fixes stick
Spend a few minutes a day on the plan on this page. Start with the Return counts, then the mark names, then the auto-punctuation choice. Once those are set, dictation needs far fewer fixes.
Change one setting at a time when a break keeps landing in the wrong place. Test again after each change. One change at a time shows you which fix worked.
Next steps

Check your macOS version under Apple menu > About This Mac. Then set Auto-punctuation in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation and test three sentences. If you want help while you work, the [download page](/download) has the Mac app, and [pricing](/pricing) lists the plans.

faq.question: What is the difference between new line and new paragraph on Mac?
faq.answer: Apple says “new line” is the same as pressing Return once. “New paragraph” is the same as pressing Return twice. The break appears when you finish dictating, so check it after each section.

faq.question: Does Mac dictation add commas and periods automatically?
faq.answer: In supported languages, Dictation inserts commas, periods, and question marks as you speak. Turn this off in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation if it misfires. Apple’s page does not list the supported languages, so check there for yours.

faq.question: Is full stop the same as period?
faq.answer: Yes. Apple lists period, point, dot, and full stop together as ways to produce a period. Pick the one that feels natural, then test it once in a blank note.

faq.question: Do I need Microsoft 365 to dictate in Word on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Microsoft says Dictate is only available to Microsoft 365 subscribers. You start it from Home > Dictate. Check Microsoft’s support page for current requirements before you rely on it.

faq.question: Can I still use Dragon for Mac?
faq.answer: Nuance discontinued Dragon Professional Individual for Mac effective 10/22/2018, according to a reseller post that quotes the Nuance notice. Nuance stopped providing updates after that. Use Apple’s Dictation or another supported tool instead.

faq.question: Does dictation work in every language?
faq.answer: No. Apple says Dictation is not available in all languages or regions. Microsoft says preview languages may have lower accuracy or limited punctuation support. Check the language list in each app before a long draft.

faq.question: Where does my audio go when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is not used to train AI models. Follow your employer’s rules for client or patient data.

costs.title: Time spent fixing the text
costs.text: Speech is faster to produce text but not to finished text. In a lab study of short messages, English speech averaged 153 WPM against 52 WPM on the keyboard. Speech also left more errors in the final text, 1.30% against 0.79%. Every missed comma costs you a second read.

costs.title: Wrong breaks in a sent document
costs.text: A stray new paragraph command can split one thought into two blocks. Your reader sees the gap before they see your point. Fixing a break before you send takes seconds. Fixing it after a client has read it takes longer and looks worse.

costs.title: Longer drafts to check
costs.text: In a randomized trial of clinical notes, speech-assisted reports were longer, 649 characters per report against 356 when typed. The authors suggest the bigger effect may be more documentation, not time saved. More text means more marks and breaks to proofread.

costs.title: A subscription for Word dictation
costs.text: Dictate in Word needs a Microsoft 365 subscription, according to Microsoft’s support page. Check Microsoft’s pricing page for current plans before you plan a workflow around it. Do not assume the feature is free in Word for Mac.

costs.title: Records that carry errors
costs.text: If a draft holds client or patient records, a wrong comma or break is still a record error. Follow your employer’s rules on which tools may process that data before you dictate a single line.

causes.title: Auto-punctuation guesses from your pauses
causes.text: Auto-punctuation has to guess where a comma or period belongs. Apple says it runs in supported languages, but its page does not explain how it guesses. Research on long-form dictation says irregular pauses and slow speakers cause segmentation and punctuation problems. Pauses in odd places produce marks in odd places.

causes.title: Mark names are literal commands
causes.text: Dictation treats mark names as commands. Dash and hyphen are separate entries in Apple’s list, with separate symbols, so saying the wrong one gives the wrong mark. Period, point, dot, and full stop all produce a period. A word you meant as plain text can also match a command.

causes.title: New line and new paragraph look alike
causes.text: Both commands start a new block, but they insert different breaks. Apple says new line is one Return and new paragraph is two. People often say new paragraph for every break, which adds gaps they do not want. The break appears only when you finish dictating, so the error can hide until later.

causes.title: Language and hardware limits
causes.text: Apple says Dictation is not available in all languages or regions. Its on-device model for spelling and punctuation covers English on M3 or later Macs with at least 12GB of unified memory. Microsoft says Word’s Dictate can have limited punctuation in preview languages. Outside those limits, test first and expect different results.

causes.title: Old Dragon installs and old guides
causes.text: Nuance discontinued Dragon Professional Individual for Mac effective 10/22/2018, according to a reseller post quoting the Nuance notice. Nuance stopped providing updates after that date. Guides that teach Dragon punctuation may not match your macOS version. Use Apple’s commands or Word’s Dictate instead.

causes.title: Long, unbroken sentences
causes.text: A paragraph spoken in one breath gives the engine few clear places to break. You then get too few periods or breaks, or breaks in the wrong place. Speaking in shorter sentences gives you more control over where marks land.

fixes.title: Say the mark name every time
fixes.text: Turn auto-punctuation off when you need exact marks. Then say each mark by its name, such as comma, period, question mark, or colon. Apple’s Commands page gives the full list. This takes a little longer per sentence, but you get the marks you meant.

fixes.title: Count your Returns
fixes.text: Say “new line” for one Return and “new paragraph” for two. Say the command at the spot where the break belongs, after the sentence before it. Check the first break in each document before you dictate the rest.

fixes.title: Turn off auto-punctuation when it misfires
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Turn off Auto-punctuation. Then dictate one sentence with a comma you say by name, and check that no extra comma appears. Keep the setting that gives you fewer fixes.

fixes.title: Dictate in short chunks
fixes.text: Speak one or two sentences, then pause. Research on long-form dictation links irregular pauses to segmentation trouble, so steady short chunks may help. I did not find a Mac study that tests this. Treat it as a practical habit, not a proven fix.

fixes.title: Use Word’s Auto Punctuation setting
fixes.text: In Word for Microsoft 365, go to Home > Dictate. Open the gear icon in the dictation settings and check the Auto Punctuation option. It can change only if your language allows it. If it is greyed out, switch languages or dictate the marks by name.

fixes.title: Save repeated blocks as snippets
fixes.text: Signatures, addresses, and standard headers contain many marks and breaks. Save each block once as a Lazur snippet and insert it by voice. You stop re-dictating the same punctuation every week, and the text stays the same each time.

fixes.title: Check your macOS version first
fixes.text: The Apple page I checked covers macOS 27. Open the Apple menu > About This Mac to see your version. On an older macOS, the commands may still work, but the punctuation model and settings can differ. Test your own Mac before you trust a guide.

fixes.title: Ask Lazur where the setting is
fixes.text: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Auto-punctuation is. Lazur draws a circle and label around the setting on your screen. You flip the switch yourself, and then you test a sentence.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Test the commands in a blank note
plan.text: Open a blank note in Pages or Word. Say each mark name from Apple’s list once. Write down which names gave you the mark you expected and which did not. Keep that list next to your keyboard for the week.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Compare auto-punctuation on and off
plan.text: Dictate the same three sentences twice, once with Auto-punctuation on and once with it off. Switch it in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. Count the marks you had to fix in each version. Keep the setting that needed fewer fixes.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Practice new line and new paragraph
plan.text: Dictate a short list, then a two-paragraph note. Use “new line” between list items and “new paragraph” between paragraphs. Move through the text with the arrow keys and check each break as you pass it.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Proofread a real draft in three passes
plan.text: Dictate one real section of your work. Read it once for marks, once for breaks, and once for meaning. Note which error type shows up most. Change one setting or command to match that error, then test again.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Set your defaults and save repeats
plan.text: Choose your Auto-punctuation default. Save signatures, addresses, and headers as snippets. Write a short rule for how you dictate, so the next draft starts from the same settings.
